REITs vs Physical Property: Why Buying a Singapore Condo in 2026 Might Be a Bad Financial Move
article:
Buying a condominium in Singapore requires a large upfront commitment.
Real estate investment trusts (REITs)
offer another way to gain exposure to income-producing property without buying a physical property.
For this comparison, let’s evaluate two options for a S$1 million allocation: buying a Singapore condo versus building a diversified portfolio across five local REITs.
The question is not simply which option can rise more in value.
It is whether owning a physical condo actually delivers better financial returns after accounting for financing costs, rental income and ongoing expenses.
The True Cost of Owning a Singapore Condo
A S$1 million condo does not really cost S$1 million upfront, nor is that the total amount you pay.
Assuming a 75% mortgage, an investor must put down S$250,000 in cash and CPF.
Adding roughly S$24,600 in buyer’s stamp duty and about S$3,000 in legal fees brings the initial cash commitment to roughly S$277,600.
Then come the ongoing holding costs.
Beyond mortgage interest, the property owner remains responsible for property tax, maintenance fees and periodic repairs.
If the unit is rented out, agent commissions and potential vacancy periods further erode income.
REITs: A Different Way to Own Property
Instead of buying a single residential unit, an investor can split S$1 million of capital equally across five Singapore REITs at S$200,000 each.

This spread provides immediate exposure across retail, commercial, industrial, logistics and healthcare assets.

These five REITs are chosen not because they offer attractive yields, but because they cover a mix of property types and businesses, with distribution growth, high occupancy and moderate gearing.
CICT’s large portfolio offers exposure to both retail and office properties.
In contrast, CLAR’s portfolio is concentrated in the industrial segment, with the REIT having exposure across business parks, logistics facilities, industrial properties, and data centres.
Unlike CICT, which is concentrated in Singapore, CLAR adopts a more diversified approach, with the US, Australia, and the UK / Europe making up 33% of its portfolio value.
CLAR’s distributable income grew 8.6% in 1H2026.
Meanwhile, MIT owns an S$8.3 billion portfolio of 135 properties across Singapore, North America, and Japan, with global data centres making up 57.2% of assets under management – its growth closely tied to the demand for AI infrastructure.
MLT’s broad tenant base of 987 customers spans 16 sectors, none accounting for more than 17% of revenue, thereby reducing concentration risk.
Finally, Parkway Life REIT offers exposure to the healthcare sector, and is the defensive play in the portfolio.
Its comparatively low gearing, plus a reliable and steady distribution history, makes it a favourite among more conservative investors.
Based on trailing 12-month distribution yields, our S$1 million portfolio would generate about S$58,400 a year.

CICT vs CapitaLand Ascendas REIT: Which CapitaLand Giant Is the Better Buy?
The Logistics Boom: Why Mapletree Logistics Trust Is a Global Powerhouse
How the Income Differs
Rental income from a condo looks attractive at first.
At a 3.5% gross rental yield, a S$1 million condo generates about S$35,000 a year.
However, that gross figure does not represent net cash in hand.
Property taxes, maintenance fees, agent fees, and vacancy gaps take a sizeable slice out of that S$35,000.
By contrast, REIT distributions represent net income generated by professionally managed property portfolios after operating expenses and borrowing costs have already been deducted at the trust level.
Why REITs Can Be More Flexible
A REIT portfolio provides more flexibility as investors are not tied to one property.
REITs are also easier to buy and sell than a physical property.
The trade-off is that REIT unit prices can move with the stock market, and distributions are not guaranteed.

Running the 10-Year Numbers
A S$1 million property growing to S$1.28 million in 10 years sounds like an easy S$280,000 profit.
But that headline number leaves out interest costs and hidden holding costs.
Assuming a 2.5% rate for both property price growth and home loan interest, here is how the numbers stack up over a decade:

While the condo lets you use bank leverage to control a S$1 million property with less upfront cash, interest costs alone swallow up over half of the property’s S$280,000 price gain.
Meanwhile, the REIT portfolio generates about 2.7 times as much net cash income over the same period, without any mortgage stress or landlord effort.
Where Physical Property Still Has an Advantage
Physical residential real estate offers benefits that REITs cannot match.
Direct leverage allows investors to control a S$1 million asset with a fraction of the capital upfront.
If property prices appreciate well beyond inflation, that leverage amplifies the return on the initial equity.
Physical property also offers utility – an owner can choose to live in the unit or pass it down to family.
The trade-off is that higher potential leveraged returns come with concentration risk, ongoing property maintenance and significant liquidity lock-ups.
Get Smart: Look Beyond the Headline Purchase Price
A S$1 million property growing to S$1.28 million in 10 years sounds like a straightforward windfall on paper, but real estate returns are defined by friction:
interest rates
, holding costs, taxes, and illiquidity.
REITs have their own risks.
But I can spread S$1 million across several property portfolios without buying and managing a physical property.
For me, the question is how much leverage, cost and concentration I am comfortable taking on for the potential return.
If the market falls further, will you be ready… or fully invested?

title: Hong Kong regulators signal tightening for distressed listed stocks
article:
(Oct 8): Hong Kong’s financial watchdogs warned they may reverse a rule that allows listed companies to keep trading even when auditors cast doubt on their ability to survive.

The Accounting and Financial Reporting Council, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) and Hong Kong Exchanges & Clearing Ltd (HKEX) issued a joint statement on Thursday threatening to reinstate trading suspensions for firm that receive a “disclaimer of opinion solely relating to going concern”.

Since the stock exchange relaxed the rule in 2019, the number of listed firms operating under such going-concern disclaimers surged to 95 in 2025 from 12 in 2017, according to the statement. Among those, 65 firms have maintained the designation for more than a year and in the most extreme case, 14 consecutive years.

The 2019 exemption was intended to protect investors from prolonged suspensions, enabling distressed issuers to raise capital or meet debt covenants. However, regulators said an audit disclaimer, even one limited to going-concern issues, means the auditor is unable to express an opinion on the overall accounts, undermining the basic reliability of financial statements.

“If no significant improvement is observed, the exchange will consider amending the listing rules as necessary, including requiring listed issuers with a disclaimer of opinion solely relating to going concern to be suspended,” the watchdogs said.

The potential crackdown highlights a balancing act for Hong Kong officials. While the city’s capital markets have seen a revival in initial public offerings alongside broader efforts to ease listing friction, regulators have grown increasingly wary of deal quality.

See also: Bain said to explore investment in Hong Kong’s New World

The SFC and HKEX previously restricted the number of transactions individual dealmakers can handle, while the audit regulator raised concerns over stretched audit firms handling an expanding list of corporate books.

title: Saudis in talks to formalise Hormuz shuttles in fight for market — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 8): Saudi Arabia is in talks with customers to offer oil loadings next year outside the Strait of Hormuz in long-term contracts, formalising a system the kingdom has been using during the Iran war as it pushes for greater market share.

Discussions are ongoing and must conclude by year end, according to people familiar with the matter. If approved, it would mark a significant change in the way Saudi Arabia sends its crude to customers, as deliveries under long-term contracts make up the bulk of the kingdom’s supply.

The war in its eighth month has sent traditional oil shipping routes into turmoil with Hormuz severely disrupted. Major Gulf exporters have been forced to adapt to keep customers satisfied, with shuttles through the strait — where the seller often takes the risk of passage and transfers cargoes to other vessels outside the waterway — emerging as a crucial system to keep markets supplied as competition for buyers picks up.

State-run Saudi Aramco is also discussing other changes, including a choice of pricing benchmarks and even delivering cargoes all the way to customers in Asia, the people said, asking not to be identified because the talks are private. No final decisions have been made, and details including pricing, freight and eligible volumes remain under discussion, they said.

Aramco and the Saudi Energy Ministry didn’t respond to requests for comments on the talks.

See also: Oil gains on report Trump may order Iran strikes before midterms

Before the conflict, Aramco’s main customers in Asia arranged vessels to collect oil they bought from the company at the Ras Tanura export terminal, deep inside the Gulf. The Saudi company generally wasn’t involved in arranging the shipping.

Since the war began, some shipowners have been reluctant to enter Hormuz, leaving buyers struggling to secure tankers at a reasonable cost even when oil is available. That gave rise to the Hormuz shuttling system that the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq have used to deliver their cargoes outside the waterway via ship-to-ship transfers.

Saudi Aramco has been supplying its three main export grades — Arab Light, Medium and Heavy — using these shuttles, the people said.

See also: Oil advances as vessel attacks challenge rising Hormuz shipments

Recently, the company has also allowed some buyers to conduct ship-to-ship transfer off the coast of India, one of the people said. That allows customers who can’t travel to the Gulf of Oman because of security issues a potentially safer option, while also helping to alleviate congestion around Arabian peninsula ports.

Aramco is also exploring ways to arrange the shipping to deliver more crude directly to customers, the people said. In addition to facilitating the flow of exports, these options could also allow Aramco to capture some of the gains from the soaring cost of hiring ships to traverse Hormuz, the people said.

Some Asian customers have also been in discussions with Aramco to potentially price long-term, contractual purchases against Brent futures instead of the Dubai and Oman benchmarks, the people said. That would also represent a new degree of flexibility from the Gulf producer.

title: NTT DC REIT’s manager aligns interest with unitholders with these steps
article:
External managers often act in the interests of the REIT’s unitholders and NTT DC REIT’s announcement underscores this aspect of the external manager model.

The manager is proposing that the performance fee be changed from a percentage of net property income to be linked to the y-o-y growth in distributions per unit (DPU). In addition, the manager is proposing to revise the issue price of units paid to the manager in the form of units for management fees to mitigate dilution.

A hurdle rate is being introduced for the performance fee. The structure will be 0.1% per annum of the deposited property where year-on-year DPU growth exceeds 3.0% but below 5.0%; or 0.2% per annum of the Deposited Property where year-on-year DPU growth is at least 5.0%. No performance fee will be payable where year-on-year DPU growth is 3.0% or less.

The REIT Manager also intends to waive its FY2026/2027 performance fee (NTT DC REIT has a March year end) if the actual FY2026/2027 DPU is less than 7.80 US cents, being the forecast DPU for FY2026/2027 as set out in its IPO prospectus dated July 7, 2025. Subject to the approval of unitholders, the proposed performance fee structure will take effect from FY2026/2027. The performance fees for FY2026/2027 shall be calculated based on the actual DPU for FY2026/2027 against the annualised DPU for FY2025/2026, a media release says.

The REIT Manager is also proposing to amend the basis for determining the issue price of units issued in payment of management fees. Under the current structure, the units are issued based on the market price. The proposed issue price will be determined as follows: where the market price is at or below the NAV, the units issued will be priced at the NAV; and where the market price is above the NAV the units issued will be priced at the market price.

Given that a higher issue price will result in fewer units being issued for the same amount of management fees, the proposed change will reduce potential dilution. This will also be subject to approval by unitholders and will take effect from Oct 1.

title: Temasek’s Seviora to integrate Azalea, SeaTown and Seviora Capital into a single platform
article:
Temasek’s asset management subsidiary, Seviora Holdings plans to integrate three of its wholly-owned asset management companies, Azalea Investment Management, SeaTown Holdings International and Seviora Capital into a single platform. The changes are set to take effect on Jan 1, 2027.

Established in 2020, Seviora Holdings was set up to serve as the operational holding company for four of Temasek’s wholly-owned or affiliated asset management companies. They include: Azalea Investment Management, Fullerton Fund Management, InnoVen Capital and SeaTown Holdings International. Pavillion Capital, another wholly-owned subsidiary of Temasek, became a part of Seviora Holdings earlier this year.

“Since Seviora was established in 2020, our asset management companies have progressively built shared capabilities across areas such as sustainability, technology, human resources, and sales and distribution” says Gabriel Lim, CEO of Seviora Holdings. Lim, a former civil servant, was appointed executive director and CEO of the company on Sept 1, 2025.

“Coming together as a single platform is the natural next step,” Lim adds. “This is an important milestone in the evolution of our group and reinforces our ambition to be a leading capital gateway between Asia and the world.”

Seviora Holdings’ combined assets under management as of June 30 was US$75.6 billion ($96.9 billion). The planned integration will not affect Fullerton Fund Management and InnoVen Capital. Both companies will continue to operate as separate legal entities within the group.

The combined business is expected to operate under the Seviora name. Seviora Holdings says it is currently conducting a review on the group’s brand and will share more details in due course.

title: StarHub takes tentative step towards industry consolidation with acquisition of MyRepublic's mobile business
article:
Just as the industry has been waiting for Keppel to finally sell M1 to StarHub so that the market repair can finally begin, StarHub has announced the acquisition of the mobile business of MyRepublic, adding potentially $2.4 million in earnings to its mobile business.

With just 85,000 active users, adding mobile business of MyRepublic is at best a tentative step towards the meaningful, long-awaited consolidation of the local mobile industry.

For years, StarHub is seen as the obvious choice to take over M1 so as to give the local mobile industry the sorely-needed consolidation.

However, M1 was sold by Keppel to Simba instead. The $1.43 billion deal was eventually spiked by the regulator and M1 is back on the table and active discussions are on-going.

StarHub is no stranger to MyRepublic. Besides the broadband business already subsumed under StarHub, there are MyRepublic's customers riding on StarHub's networks too.

According to StarHub, the net profit before tax attributable to MyRepublic's mobile business for the year ended June 30 is $2.4 million. The 85,000 active subscribers generate an average revenue per user of $13 per month.

See also: Ellisons invest about US$17 bil in Warner Bros takeover

The deal is targeted for completion by April 30 2027.

How much StarHub will pay for this deal will be based on a formula that takes into account data points, including the number of active subscribers on both the 5G and 4G networks, how long these subscribers are with MyRepublic etc.

"With ongoing consolidation, we are bringing greater scale to invest more effectively in the networks, resilience and innovation that Singapore will increasingly depend on.

See also: Ellison’s new Skydance seeks to wring more profits from movies

"This transaction strengthens those foundations while continuing to give consumers meaningful choice in how they connect,” says StarHub CEO Nikhil Eapen.

Matt Williams, StarHub's CEO-designate calls this deal a "strong fit" to the company's multi-brand, multi-segment strategy.

"Different customers want different things from their mobile experience, and our approach allows us to offer distinct brands and propositions while giving more customers access to the strength of StarHub’s network," he adds.

Vaughan Baker, MyRepublic's group CEO says that "nothing changes" for his customers and that "continuity and quality of service remain our main priority.

title: SK Hynix’s flash memory unit said to pick banks for US IPO next year
article:
(Oct 8): SK Hynix Inc’s Solidigm has picked lead banks for its US initial public offering (IPO) next year, according to people familiar with the matter.

The South Korean firm’s flash memory unit selected Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley to work on the offering, which could raise about US$10 billion ($12.8 billion), the people said. Separately, Solidigm is working with the two lenders to finalise a pre-IPO funding round, the people said.

JPMorgan Chase & Co, Citigroup Inc and UBS Group AG have also been tapped for Solidigm’s IPO, the people said. A listing could take place as soon as 2027 and value the company at as much as US$100 billion, Bloomberg News has reported.

Deliberations are ongoing, details could change and more banks may be added, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. Reuters was first to report the size of the offering.

A spokesperson for SK Hynix said its subsidiary Solidigm is reviewing various options to strengthen its business competitiveness, but no specific plans have been confirmed at this time. Representatives of Solidigm, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan and Citigroup declined to comment. UBS didn’t respond to requests for comments.

The second-largest memory firm’s American depositary receipts fell 4.3% last Friday as a lock-up agreement on insiders selling shares lifted following its US$26.5 billion listing in July, the biggest ever for a non-US company.

See also: Nvidia-backed Firmus said to close books as IPO struggles — Bloomberg

The pace of US IPOs has slowed despite a string of megadeals, with companies including smart ringmaker Oura joining a handful of others postponing their expected debuts in recent weeks. While Anthropic PBC is expected to go public before the US Thanksgiving holiday, other companies are aiming for listings next year including its artificial intelligence rival OpenAI and flash memory maker Kioxia Holdings Corp.

Solidigm was introduced in 2021 after SK Hynix acquired Intel Corp’s flash memory business and renamed it. The unit of the South Korean company has recast itself as a provider of high-capacity drives used in AI data centres.

In August, Solidigm struck a deal with CoreWeave Inc to sell enterprise solid-state drive capacity which could support its AI cloud platform. Other customers include Vast Data, Dell Technologies Inc and Tencent Holdings Ltd, according to the website.

See also: Deluge Corporation Limited launches IPO at 60 cents each, aims to raise gross proceeds of $23.4 million

Rancho Cordova, California-based Solidigm has 13 locations globally, including in Mexico, Canada and China, and has more than 2,000 employees.

title: Tencent mulls US$5 bil bond offering as AI push ramps up
article:
(Oct 8): Tencent Holdings Ltd is considering an offshore bond sale of as much as US$5 billion ($6.4 billion), according to people familiar with the matter, adding to the wave of tech companies seeking debt financing as artificial intelligence (AI) needs grow.

The notes could be denominated in dollars and offshore yuan and the sale may come as early as this month, the people said, asking not to be identified because the discussions are private.

While no details were available on how the money would be used, the development comes after Tencent raised nearly US$4.7 billion from the sale of long-dated dollar and yuan securities in June, in its largest debt offering since 2020. Proceeds from that deal were mainly for debt refinancing and general corporate purposes, such as developing AI products and services.

The potential bond sale adds to a global fundraising rush by tech companies as they seek to build up their AI capabilities, despite rising investor concerns about the sector. Just last month, SoftBank Group Corp raised the equivalent of US$11.1 billion through the one of the largest corporate junk-bond offerings on record in an effort to fund its massive AI ambitions.

SoftBank’s deal was seen by some as a litmus test for how debt investors are thinking about AI financing amid warnings about the technology’s potential risks and the need to impose guardrails around its development.

See also: Alibaba chairman says open source is Europe’s best shot at AI

Global AI-related debt issuance has already topped US$575 billion in 2026, according to a recent report by Goldman Sachs Group Inc credit strategists, despite worries about potential consequences for markets if the technology fails to pay off for firms making the biggest investments.

Tencent has around US$22 billion of offshore notes outstanding and no public bonds maturing this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. It has one dollar bond due in 2028.

The company has been ramping up its AI-related spending as it tries to catch up to rivals such as ByteDance Ltd and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, raising capital expenditures by 176% on AI projects and computing to 52.8 billion yuan (US$7.9 billion or $10.1 billion) in the June quarter.

See also: MAS sets AI risk expectations for financial institutions in Singapore

Tencent aims to develop AI models akin to the best from DeepSeek or Moonshot AI, such as the Hy4 for later in 2026. It already operates one of the country’s largest Amazon Web Services-like cloud services, offering computing to clients keen to develop their own AI platforms.
